Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally out, but if you're a sci-fi aficionado looking for similar experiences set in outer space, there are several alternatives.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time. Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans?

To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space.

The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons.

The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games.

With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars.

Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics.

Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it.

The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining.

Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky.

It's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns with alien NPCs, gigantic kaiju-like beasts, and... fishing. The endless free updates have pushed the roleplaying aspects deeper, as Hello Games are really making it the "forever" space game.

Most importantly though, you can be the greatest bad guy the virtually infinite universe has ever seen, controlling entire pirate fleets and firing on (or stealing) every spaceship that you come across. It might be a bit aimless for some, but if you love a "forever game" then NMS can be the biggest space-set criminal sim ever created.

Though it took too long, Star Wars has gotten really close to cracking the GTA formula in outer space in a shameless enough way. 2024's Star Wars Outlaws is, to this date, the closest thing we've received to a space-set sandbox directly inspired by Rockstar's huge hits.

By letting us fully embrace the Han Solo-like scoundrel fantasy, Massive Entertainment delivered a Star Wars adventure that's all about breaking the law. Hell, they even got a wanted system in there that has protagonist Kay Vess dodging stormtroopers and rival criminal factions like you would in Vice City.

Star Wars Outlaws' take on GTA isn't just about the surface-level gameplay and open structure; it also understands much of its playful tone, moral ambiguity, and stressful rhythm. Jumping between several medium-sized maps set on different planets and spaceship sections breaks up the experience a little, so it never quite reaches that level of seamless immersion, but if anyone wants to do a focused version of GTA in space in the future, Massive's attempt is the one game that got at least halfway there.

Before we go (and before you go back to playing GTA VI), we should remember the daring video games that, for a variety of reasons, never got to realize their visions of a crime-oriented space adventure.

Remember Star Wars 1313 and Visceral Games' cancelled project? It's hard not to spot some of their DNA surviving in Outlaws. As Luke Skywalker wisely said before noping out, "No one's ever really gone." Lucasfilm loves that, and it extends to binned video games too, thankfully. Even the elusive Battlefront 3 is back from the dead now.

Bethesda also had something going at some point with "Prey 2", a bounty hunter action game set in a cyberpunk-ish alien world. Before it was canned, it dropped one of the coolest CG game trailers ever made and teased us with a Blade Runner-esque future long before Cyberpunk hit our consoles.

Looking at the future, Ubisoft's Beyond Good & Evil 2 wants to go big and lawless, potentially iterating on Star Wars Outlaws and other open-world crime sims. But years after its announcement and many mind-boggling development news updates, it's hard to believe it's really ever coming out. Maybe the "Before GTA VI" meme can morph into "Before BG&E2" now that Rockstar's masterpiece is finally out.

Ultimately, Rockstar is Rockstar. A one-of-a-kind megastudio with nearly unlimited resources. Trying to replicate GTA does — either on Earth or among the stars — would be an Icarus flight in the making for most studios. There are some GTA-flavored space adventures out there, as we've shown, but we're still waiting for the one. Something that matches the deep storytelling, complete freedom, and cheeky tone of Rockstar's iconic series. OK, I gotta get out of here, I'm too hip for this, I gotta play GTA VI some more.

Jason and Lucia have always known the deck is stacked against them. But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a criminal conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida — forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. #629. BepiColombo finally reaches Mercury after eight-year odyssey

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

False-colour view of Mercury produced using data from MESSENGER.Credit: NASA Goddard

After an epic eight-year journey, the European and Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has arrived at Mercury. It is only the second mission — after NASA’s MESSENGER in 2011–2015 — to enter orbit around the innermost planet of the Solar System.

On 21 November, the European Space Agency (ESA) announced that a European-built module had inserted itself into Mercury’s orbit, beginning a months-long series of manoeuvres. In the coming weeks, its two scientific probes — one built by ESA and the other by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will separate, allowing each to follow its own orbit at a different altitude.

En route to Mercury the craft was able to test some of its onboard instruments. Mission scientists pointed the onboard X-ray camera, the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), at the Crab Nebula, the remnants of a supernova witnessed on Earth in 1054. MIXS is the first X-ray imaging device to be sent on an interplanetary mission, says Emma Bunce, a plasma physicist at the University of Leicester, UK, who is one of BepiColombo’s leading mission scientists.

For the time being, the two probes will remain conjoined, until they reach the prescribed orbit for the JAXA probe, called MIO, on 9 December. It will trace ellipses at altitudes between 500 km and 11,000 km, sampling the planet’s magnetic field and how it interacts with solar wind. The ESA-built probe, which is called Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and carries MIXS, among other instruments, will then gradually descend until March 2027, when it will reach its orbit at between 400–1,500 km. From there, its instruments will continuously study the planet’s surface.

The BepiColumbo spacecraft (illustration).Credit: ESA - P. Carril

Travelling to the Solar System’s innermost regions is a “prolonged affair”, Bunce says. “Energetically, it takes more energy to go to Mercury than to go to the outer Solar System,” says Bunce. BepiColombo launched in October 2018, and needed to gradually lower itself closer to the Sun without gaining speed and overshooting Mercury.

A lunar gold rush could destroy the valuable lunar environment and obscure valuable scientific material.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material.

Both China and the U.S. are pushing forward with plans to establish permanent human settlements on the moon by the end of the next decade. Commercial players want to build businesses supporting these future explorers by mining for resources such as water, construction materials, industrial metals and rare earth minerals.

However, some scientists argue that a temporary ban on lunar industrialization is necessary to allow regulations to catch up and limit what can be allowed in order to prevent a moon rush from destroying the pristine lunar environment.

Two such researchers are Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. In a piece published last month in the journal Global Environmental Politics, the pair call for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to allow the global community to carefully consider the impact of economic activities on the moon.

In addition to the threat to the scientifically priceless lunar landscape, the researchers also object to the colonization of the moon by a small number of powerful players — namely China, the U.S. and their respective close allies.

"With the moon it's absolutely clear that whoever is doing the big infrastructure work is going to be asserting their position, including by defining their own exclusive territories," Rabitz said in a statement. "That shouldn't be the Wild West."

Rabitz pointed out that, although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prevents individual nations from appropriating the moon, Earth's natural satellite and its valuable resources are unlikely to remain truly neutral territory if its exploitation is going to be led by a small number of powerful nations.

Tereza is a London-based science and technology journalist, aspiring fiction writer and amateur gymnast. #627. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

#626. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit.

The 42,000-pound module is called Zarya, and it's about the size of a tour bus. Zarya launched on board a Russian Proton rocket. Two weeks later, NASA's STS-88 shuttle mission aboard Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit.

Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station.

Today, the International Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze.

As of this writing, the International Space Station is 28 years old, and has seen steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000 (for 26 years and counting). It is a marvel of space engineering, but every engineering marvel begins the same: with the first piece.

And that is what the Zarya module is: The foundation of the International Space Station.

Zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block (or Russian acronym FGB), is the core module of the space station around which every other module was attached. It weighed 42,600 pounds at launch and is just aver 41 feet long and 13.5 feet wide. Inside, it boasts a total habitable volume of 1,650 cubic feet.

NASA paid $220 million for Zarya's construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow, with work beginning in 1994 and ending in 1998. The module is a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs, with two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks to store propellant.

While NASA's space shuttle Endeavour was the first to meet Zarya (and attach NASA's core Unity connecting module to it), it wasn't until Russia'z Zvezda service launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya's aft that the fledgling space station was large enough to accomodate its first three-person crew, Expedition 1.

Over the last 28 years, giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings and many other modules (built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada and Japan) have greatly expanded the living area of the station. Many ISS components could not be tested with one another on the ground, meaning the first time they were attached was in space during construction.

The result is a feat of space construction that has only recently seen a rival as China works to expand its own Tiangong space station.

Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube.

#624. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

The scale of the economic disruption caused by AI has led even conservative politicians to talk about universal basic income. But economists aren't convinced, and campaigners think we need to ask deeper questions.

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

"I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he said, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these issues in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently."

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

Nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail company, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market."

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play."

The idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they said AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

But Herrmann said it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

"On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she said. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens."

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

However, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living."

Other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," said Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible."

Kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

For her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?"

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," said Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?"

#623. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

NROL-105 | USSF-385 | 8 Starlink missions

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

#621. Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

Events were held for "Volkstrauertag," a day commemorating victims of war and oppression. Meanwhile, experts said the country is headed for a budget crisis.

This live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he said.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he said, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he said.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police said.

Officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police launched a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

St. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

"This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown said before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

"I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in."

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police said the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

The bar said it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk."

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other issues.

Police said there had been some clashes with participants.   A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country."

Steinmeier said he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic."

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many important biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg said ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police said on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then said to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement said.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

"Democracy is the antidote here," she said. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom."

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

Read on here for the top stories from and about Germany on Sunday, November 15,

It's 1 a.m. here and time for us to pause our coverage of news from Germany.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

#620. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

It's a moment more than eight years in the making.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth.

The BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.

The big moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes.

BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018, beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system.

Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun. Spacecraft approaching the solar system's innermost planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug.

So the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year, however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters.

Today's orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total.

Arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts.

Shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027.

BepiColombo won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their two different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world.

"The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description.

"The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added.

#618. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

"In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk said on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship launches to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.)

Musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.)

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the company had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how important this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

And SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the company wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that new Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which launched on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.
